home.lead: {projects} projects, {techs} technologies, one common thread: 3D meshes and their topology. Each project is generated with AI, then reviewed, tested and documented by me.
home.thread.title: The common thread
home.thread.text: One mesh runs through the whole portfolio: read in C, analysed in C++, served by a Python API, classified by an ML model, measured in SQL, described in a toy language and displayed in React, Angular and Qt.

method.estimation.text: Two scales: projects in points (3, 5, 8 or 13, revised when the scope changes, as the roguelike went from 8 to 13 points), stories in points from 1 to 4. Observed capacity: {mean} story points per sprint on average, from {min} to {max}; each sprint's commitment follows that capacity, and {delivered} of the {committed} committed points were delivered. At the planned pace, the {remaining} points left fit in sprints {next} to {last}.
method.retro.text: At the end of each sprint, three questions: what worked, what the AI got wrong, what to change in the next sprint. Charles writes the answers in the sprint's file, and the decisions they lead to go to DECISIONS.md.
method.genai.steps: Specification|Reviewed architecture plan|Tests first, generation in small steps|Check that a test fails when the code is broken|Review of every diff|Green CI on Linux, Windows and macOS before merge|REVIEW.md and DECISIONS.md updated

gcartes.title: Mini-course: generalized maps
gcartes.lead: Six short lessons on the structure of my thesis, an unfolded cube to explore dart by dart, and a quiz to check.
gcartes.figure.alt: Net of the cube: six squares, each with its 8 darts, and the letters a to h of the cube's vertices.
gcartes.figure.caption: The unfolded cube: each segment is a dart, the dot marks its vertex; α0 in black, α1 in red, α2 in blue (between squares next to each other in the net; click a dart to see all its links). The same letter is the same vertex of the cube.
gcartes.figure.start: Click a dart, or use the α buttons to move.
gcartes.noscript: The figure and the quiz are interactive with JavaScript; the lessons read without it.
gcartes.label.counts: Counted as orbits: {darts} darts, {vertices} vertices, {edges} edges, {faces} faces, χ = {euler}.
gcartes.legend: Key: α0 links in black, α1 in red, α2 in blue.
gcartes.step.0.title: The object.
gcartes.step.0.text: Two squares sharing an edge: 2 faces, 7 edges, 6 vertices.
gcartes.step.1.title: Cut by α2.
gcartes.step.1.text: The faces come apart; an α2 link (blue) remembers the edge they shared.
gcartes.step.2.title: Cut by α1.
gcartes.step.2.text: Each face falls into its sides; α1 links (red) remember the corners. The shared edge is now sewn at each of its ends.
gcartes.step.3.title: Cut by α0.
gcartes.step.3.text: Each side splits into two darts; an α0 link (black) joins the two halves. 16 darts and their links remain: that is the G-map.

parbench.title: Benchmarks
parbench.lead: The same curvature, computed by each version on tori from 50,000 to 3.2 million triangles; median time, adjacency already built, copies to the graphics card included.
parbench.machine: Measured on {cpu} ({threads} OpenMP threads on {logical} logical processors), graphics card {gpu}, under WSL 2; median of {runs} runs.
parbench.transfers: On the graphics card, in double precision: {upload} ms copying to the card, {kernels} ms computing, {download} ms back, and {host} ms on the processor (allocations). In single precision the computation alone drops to {floatKernels} ms: this consumer card has 32 times fewer double-precision units than single-precision ones. For a single curvature the copies are what costs: computing on the card pays off when the data stays there.
parbench.float: Single precision strays by at most {error} on an angle defect: enough to show colours, not to check Gauss-Bonnet to the millionth.
parbench.memory: Why OpenMP is not six times faster: the vertex pass reads a lot of memory for little computation, and the bandwidth of this machine under WSL tops out at 5 to 6 GB/s whatever the number of threads (measured); the face pass, for its part, runs 4.5 times faster on 6 cores. With 12 threads, the ones spinning while they wait on the logical cores slow the others down: one thread per physical core is faster here.

bataille.title: What 100,000 games say
bataille.lead: The Ada program played the {games} games of seeds 1 to 100,000, up to 10,000 plies each; the figures come from its output file, recomputed by CI.

bataille.plies: plies on average when the game ends
bataille.first: of the finished games won by the first player
bataille.range: plies from the shortest to the longest
bataille.why: Why so many endless games? Here the winner of a trick always picks the cards up in the same order: the game becomes deterministic and can cycle. Between real players the order changes from trick to trick and the game nearly always ends.
